query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Microsegregation and residual porosity inherent to the as-built additive manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA lead to non-uniform diffusion paths and local variations in reactive element concentrations, which in turn cause uneven and poorly adherent high-temperature oxide scale formation. This heterogeneous oxide scale under oxidizing or reducing environments accumulates localized stresses that accelerate spallation and can trigger catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additive manufactured HEA with an FCC matrix exhibiting microsegregation and detectable porosity.
generation.intervention: Apply a homogenization heat treatment aimed at reducing microsegregation and minimizing porosity.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., 900–1000 °C) in controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres over extended durations (e.g., thermal cycling or 100-hour isothermal tests).
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform microstructure with reduced compositional gradients and fewer porosity defects.
generation.mechanism: The homogenized microstructure promotes uniform diffusion of reactive species, leading to the formation of a continuous and adherent oxide scale that minimizes local stress accumulation and spallation. Conversely, the as-built microstructure fosters localized oxide growth variations and differential diffusion, which result in stress concentrations and eventual scale failure that precipitates catastrophic degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built baseline, homogenized samples will exhibit a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scale with improved resistance to spallation under high-temperature oxidizing/reducing conditions, thereby delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: As-built, microsegregated HEA samples that develop irregular oxide scales with early signs of spallation and accelerated degradation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within high-temperature regimes (approximately 900–1000 °C) under both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres where diffusion and oxidation kinetics are actively governing scale formation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative degree to which homogenization improves scale adhesion and reduces interfacial stresses is uncertain, as is the precise impact on long-term cyclic degradation under varying gas compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples: one set as-built and one set subjected to a homogenization heat treatment. Expose both sets to high-temperature (950 °C) environments in controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres over a duration sufficient for oxide scale development (e.g., 100 hours or 100 thermal cycles). Conduct detailed cross-sectional microscopy, EDS mapping, and mechanical scratch tests to assess oxide-scale uniformity, thickness, and adhesion, along with mass change measurements to monitor degradation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM and EDS)
Adhesion strength and spallation resistance (via scratch testing and thermal cycling data)
Onset of catastrophic failure through mechanical testing and fractography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity, adherence, and reduced degradation (as measured by slower mass change and delayed catastrophic failure) compared to the as-built samples under the same exposure conditions, then the hypothesis that microsegregation governs the degradation mechanism leading to catastrophic failure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Beyond conventional alloying, the addition of trace reactive elements, particularly yttrium (Y), has been widely recognized as one of the most effective routes for improving the long-term stability of alumina-forming alloys. This behavior, commonly referred to as the reactive element effect (REE), is generally associated with modified oxide-growth mechanisms, suppressed cation outward diffusion, and enhanced oxide-scale adhesion. According to the dynamic segregation theory [,,], reactive-element ions preferentially segregate to oxide grain boundaries, thereby reducing outward metal-ion diffusion and mitigating growth stress within the scale. In addition, Y-containing oxides may form discrete interfacial anchoring sites, often described as oxide pegs, which mechanically stabilize the scale and inhibit spallation during repeated thermal cycling [,]. Although the REE has been extensively investigated in conventional Ni- and Fe-based superalloys, its interaction with the chemically complex multi-principal-element matrix of HEAs remains insufficiently understood [,]. cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents the mechanical stability analysis of the oxide scales. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy. It is worth mentioning that all the prior studies on microstructural refinement and the oxidation behavior of the resulting materials were limited to conventional structural materials only. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, there has been no study on achieving remarkable oxidation resistance in HEAs through microstructural refinement. In the current work, microstructural refinement of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA was accomplished via severe surface deformation using stationary friction processing (SFP). The processing resulted in ultrafine-grain structure with a significant fraction of nanograins in the as-cast HEA along with significant elemental homogenization. The processed HEA samples demonstrated exceptional oxidation resistance, and the reported mass gain values are among the lowest for the investigated HEA. The remarkable performance of the processed HEAs was attributed to the formation of an intact, dense, uniformly distributed oxide scale, favored by large grain boundary density, higher surface free energy, and uniform elemental distribution.
